WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
Collapse of newly built highways in eastern India 
*161. SHRIS.S.AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, 
ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are seized of the incidents of portions of 
newly-built highways under the Golden Quadrilateral Project (GQP) caving 
in certain parts of the eastern India, in particular; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that NHAI has adopted uniform technical 
parameters for laying roads under the GQP throughout the country in 
disregard to the varied geological formations and soil texture prevailing in 
different parts; 
(d) if so, the rationale therefor; 
(e) whether any investigation into the reasons for collapse of sections 
of GQP highways have been carried out and accountability fixed; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
4 

[2 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) About 110 metre portion of the Kharagpur side embankment on the 
right hand side approach road to Road Over Bridge in Km. 19 of National 
Highway No. 6 in West Bengal subsided on 09.02.2006. 
(c) and (d) No, Sir. Detailed survey and soil investigations are carried 
out for individual projects and designs of various road features are made by 
specialised consultants, keeping in view the site conditions and specific local 
requirements to achieve the prescr ibed standards. The standards are 
contained in the norms/guidelines of Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport 
& Highways, Indian Roads Congress and Bureau of Indian Standards. In the 
absence of any specific norms the international norms are followed. 
(e) and (0 National Highways Authority of India has constituted an 
Enquiry Committee comprising former Director General (Road 
Development), Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport & Highways and 
professor of IIT Kharagpur who is Geo-Technical expert, to investigate the 
reasons and circumstances leading to fa ilure of the approach road of ROB 
and to suggest remedial measures.

Repayment of loans to Asian Development Bank 
*163.     SHRI JAI PARKASH AGGARWAL: 
SHRIAJAYMAROO: 
Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the National Highway Authority of India 
has defaulted in repayment of loans to the Asian Development Bank; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the action taken/proposed to be taken against the officers 
responsible for this lapse? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) and (b) National Highways 
Authority of India (NHAI) repaid the first instalment of Asian Development 
Bank (ADB) Loan amounting to US $ 43,08,820.36 (Rs. 19,14,40,889) for 
Surat-Manor Tollway Project on 10.01.2006, 9 days beyond the due date of 
01.01.2006. The delay was due to lapse on part of the concerned officers. 
(c) A fact finding enquiry has investigated into this lapse and based on 
the enquiry, one Dy. General Manage r (Finance & Accounts) has been 
placed under suspension and one General Manager (Finance & Accounts) 
who was on deputation to the NHAI, has been repatriated to the parent 
organization. 
Implementation of Central Right to Information Act 
*164.     SHRIMATIHEMAMALINI: 
SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have ensured that the Central Right to 
Information Act is being implemented throughout the country; 
(b) whether any States are lagging behind; and

(c) if so, which are these States and what steps are being taken to ask 
those States for its immediate implementation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCESAND PENSIONS (SHRISURESH PACHOURI): 
(a) to (c) The Central Government has already taken action for the 
implementation of various provisions of the Act by public authorities under 
it. The State Governments also are u nder a statutory obligation to ensure 
compliance with the provisions of the Act. The Central Government, 
however, has requested the State Gove rnments to ensure speedy and full 
implementation of the Act by public authorities under their control. 
According to information presently  available 17 State Governments 
have set up State Information Commissions and made appointments thereto. 
Efforts will continue to be made by the Central Government to persuade all 
State Governments to ensure full compliance with the provisions of the Act.

Criticism of Power Incentive Scheme 
*166.      SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: 
SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Planning Commission had criticized the Power 
Incentive Scheme, in so far as it did not benefit the consumer but the 
importer of power equipments/appliances only, by way of reduction in 
customs tariff; and 
(b) if so, Government's response thereto by way of reviewing and 
revising the power policy so as to benefit the consumer, directly? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) 
No, Sir. As a matter of fact, there is no "Power Incentive Scheme". However, 
under the Mega Power Policy announced in 1995 and modified in 1998, for 
large projects, benefits of custom duty and excise duty waivers are available. 
The question was referred to Planning Commission also who have responded 
that they are unaware of any Planning Commission document in which such 
a criticism was made. Under the Mega Power Policy, organizations like 
NTPC Ltd. have set up projects with exemption of custom duty and excise 
duty and the entire benefit of reduced ta riff as a result of such waiver has 
been transferred to consumer. 
(b) In light of (a) above, the question does not arise.

Completion of Golden Quadrilateral Scheme 
† *167.   DR. PRABHATHAKUR: 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
Will the Minister of SHIP PING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Golden Quadrilateral Scheme for National Highways 
would be completed within the stipulated time; 
(b) if not, the reasons for the delay; 
(c) whether Government propose to award incentive to those who 
complete road projects within time and penalize those who delay completion 
thereof; and. 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) and (b) It is expected that 96% 
Golden Quadrilateral Project would be completed by June 2006. The delays 
in some contracts are due to problems  associated with acquisition of land, 
shifting of utilities, environment & forest clearances, law and order, poor 
performance of contractors etc. 
(c) and (d) Provision of bonus for early completion and penalty for

*170. SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: Will the Minister of SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether predictions of monsoon, earthquakes, energy, healthcare and 
water management have become vital for the overall development of the 
country; 
(b) if so, what strenous efforts are in the pipeline of making accurate and 
timely predictions; and; 
(c) by when these would start giving their results? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ AND THE MINISTER OF 
YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to 
(c) Accurate prediction of monsoon is important for economic growth of the 
country. For monsoon prediction, there are two types of models, statistical 
and dynamical. IMD has been using a statistical model developed 
indigenously over the years. IMD is also preparing experimental long range forecast 
based on dynamical model and is continuously testing the efficiency of 
dynamical models in making acurate predictions. However, more research is 
required and efficacy of the dynamic models will only be determined when the 
forecasts prepared through this model are compared with actual observations 
over a period of time. 
Though capability to correctly predict earthquakes can minimize loss 
of life and property, however, at present there is no specific technique 
available anywhere in the world to predict the occurrence of earthquakes with 
reasonable degree of accuracy with regard to space, time & magnitude. India 
Meteorological Department (IMD) monitors earthquakes and provides 
timely information to concerned officials for rescue and relief. Government 
of India has taken up initiatives for conducting research in Earthquake 
Precursory studies through multi-parametric geophysical observations in a 
multi-institutional mode. These efforts are expected to lead to the development of 
models for earthquake prediction in future. 
As far as the area of energy, healthcare and water management are 
concerned they are vital for the overall development of the country. However, it 
is difficult to understand the import of the predictions in these areas. Scientific 
research and development is an ongoing process, which

Rank in Human Development Index 
*172. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India ranks 127th out of the 177 countries, for the 
second year in a row, on the Human Development Index of the United 
Nations; 
(b) if so, what are the determinant norms, parameters and criteria laid 
down, for determining the index; 
(c) what is the status of India, pertaining to each of the said norms, 
parameters and criteria, at present; and 
(d) what steps Government propose to take to improve Indian 
scenario regarding its position on the UN Human Development Index 
and the targets contemplated thereunder? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) Ye s, Sir, India rank 127 out of 177 
countries, as per the Human Development Reports (HDR) 2004 and 2005, prepared 
by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). These are independent 
estimates of UNDP using their own norms. 
(b) The Human Development Index (HDI) is a summary measure of 
human development. It measures the average achievements in a country in 
three basic dimensions of human development: 
(i)   A long and healthy life, as measured by life expectancy at birth. 
(ii) Knowledge, as measured by the adult literacy rate (with two-thirds 
weight) and the combined primary, secondary and tertiary gross 
enrolment ratio (with one-third weight). 
(iii) A decent standard of living, as  measured by GDP per capita (PPP 
US$). 
Before calculating the HDI, an index needs to be created for each of these 
dimensions. To calculate these dimension indices—the life expectancy, 
education and GDP indices-minimum and maximum values are chosen for each 
underlying indicator. Performance in each dimension is expressed as a value 
between 0 and 1. The HDI is then calculated as a simple average of the 
dimension indices. 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [2 March, 2006] 
(c) The overall status of India as measured by the HDI is 0.602 out 
of a maximum value of 1. Of the three criteria comprising the HDI, India's 
position is 0.64 in the Life Expectancy Index, 0.61 in the Education Index 
and 0.56 in the GDP Index. 
(d) The Government recognizes  the importance of human 
development in development planning and in view of this the Tenth Plan 
has laid down specific monitorable targets for a few key indicators of 
human development along with the target for growth rate of GDP. These 
targets are considered as central to attainment of the objectives of Tenth 
Plan. The Government, both in the Centre and in the States have initiated 
a number of programmes to improve h ealth and educational status of 
the people, as also to provide opportunities for employment and enhanced 
incomes. In order to improve literacy and universal enrolment, investment 
in education has been increased substantially both for the Sarva Siksha 
Abhiyan and for universal coverage under the mid-day meal scheme. 
Similarly, in the health sector, there has been step up in investment with 
a new thrust on rural health (The Na tional Rural Health Mission). In order 
to improve the level of living of the people, rapid economic growth with 
social justice is envisaged in the pl anning process. The Tenth Five Year 
Plan (2002—07) target a GDP growth rate of 8% per year. The emphasis 
is on agriculture development and on labour-intensive sectors, which 
would generate greater employment in the growth process. In addition, 
there are specially targeted anti-poverty programmes for the poor and 
disadvantaged groups. Improving delivery and governance are also 
receiving attention of the Government. These initiatives are expected to 
improve the various indicators used in the UN Human Development Index 
to provide the basic aspects of human development in the country.

below poverty line according to 1999-2000 data (page no. 2, Table No. 1.1 of the Report). 
It may be mentioned that this figure is taken from the official poverty estimates 
brought out by the Planning Commission on the basis of NSS 55th round of large scale 
sample survey on household consumer expenditure, which was conducted during the 
year 1999-2000. The state-wise details of incident of poverty by official methodology of 
Planning Commission is given in Statement-I. (See below) 
(c) The Government has adopted a three pronged strategy for reducing poverty 
(i) acceleration of economic growth with a focus on sectors which are employment 
intensive; (ii) human and social development through provision of basic 
minimum services; and (iii) targeted anti poverty programmes. 
The details of the Schemes/programmes made and being 
72 

[2 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
implemented by the Union Government in the country to eliminate poverty are as 
follows: 
In rural areas the programmes which are being implemented by the 
Ministry of Rural Development for tipliftment of BPL families are (i) 
Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY), (ii) Swaranajayanti Gram Swarozgar 
Yojana (SGSY), (iii) Indira Awas Yojana (IAY), (iv) National Food for Works 
Programme (NFFWP) and (v) National Rural Employment Guarantee Act. A note 
on the Rural Poverty Alleviation Programmes is at Statement-ll. (See below) 
In urban areas, with a view to ameliorate the living conditions of the 
urban poor, and to reduce the urban poverty in the country, Ministry of Urban 
Employment & Poverty Alleviation is implementing an employment 
oriented Centrally Sponsored urban poverty alleviation programme namely 
Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) on all India baiss w.e.f. 
1.12.1997. This programme seeks to provide gainful employment to the urban 
unemployed or underemployed poor through setting up of micro enterprises 
and also through provision of Wage Employment by utilizing their labour for 
construction of useful public asets. There is another programme called 'Valmiki 
Ambedkar Awas Yojana' (VAMBAY) which was introduced in 2001-02 to 
meet the long-standing gap in programmes for slum-dwellers, viz. provision 
of a shelter or upgrading the existing shelter of people living below the 
poverty line in urban slums. National Slum Development Programme (NSDP) is 
an ACA scheme under the State Sect or meant for providing shelter and 
environmental upgradation for the urban slum dwellers. A note on Urban 
Poverty Alleviation Programmes/Schemes is given as Statement-Ill. (See below) 
In Addition to this, the Public Distribution System in India has been more 
focused and targeted towards the very  poor category. The "Antyodaya Anna 
Yojana" provides 35 kgs of foodgrains to the poorest of the poor families at a 
highly subsidized rate of Rs. 2 per kg., for wheat and Rs. 3 per kg., for rice. 
Recently, the coverage of Antyodaya A nna Yojana has been  expanded from 
2.0 crore (BPL) families to 2.5 crore families in 2005. The State Governments 
have been advised to give priority to the households from the poorest and the 
backward blocks and/or where nutritional deficiency is more widespread, while 
identifying the beneficiaries.

Statement-ll 
Note on Rural Poverty Alleviation Programme/Schemes 
(i) SWARNAJAYANTI GRAM SWAROZGAR YOJANA (SGSY) 
The Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yo jana (SGSY) is an integrated 
programme for self-employment of the rural poor launched on 1 April 1999 
following the restructuring of the erstwhile Integrated Rural Development 
Programme (IRDP) and allied schemes. The objective of the SGSY is to bring 
the assisted poor families (Swarozgaris) above the poverty line by organising 
them into self-help groups (SHGs), training them and helping them in 
capacity building and provision of income generating assets through bank 
credit and government subsidy. Other important com ponents of the 
programme are: development of infrastructure, establishment of marketing 
linkages and providing technological support. The programme has in-built 
safeguards for the weaker sections with 50 per cent benefits reserved for 
scheduled castes/ scheduled tribes (SC/ST). In addition, 50 per cent of the 
groups formed in each block are expected to be exclusively for women who will 
account for at least 40 per cent of the Swarozgaris. 
(ii) NATIONAL RURAL EMPLOYMENT GUARANTEE ACT 
(NREGA) 
The Government has enacted National Rural Employment Guarantee 
Act (NREGA) in September, 2005. The Act guarantees 100 days of 
employment in a financial year to any rural household whose adult members 
are willing to do unskilled manual work. The Act will be applicable to areas 
notified by the Central Government and will cover the whole country within five 
years. In the first phase, the NREGA has been launched on 2nd February, 2006 
in 200 districts across the country, out of which 150 are those where National 
Food For Work Programme (NFFWP) was in existence and 50 other Districts 
have been identified. 
The National Rural Employment Guar antee Act aims to enhance the 
livelihood security of the people in rural areas by generating wage 
employment through works that develop the infrastructure base of that area. 
The choice of works suggested addresses causes of chronic poverty like drought, 
deforestation, soil erosion. The Act envisages a collaborative partnership between 
the Centre and State Governments, the Panchayats and the local community. The 
Panchayats at each level are the "Principal 
76 

[2 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Authorities for Planning, Implementation and Monitoring of the Act". Gram 
Panchayat is responsible for planning, registering, issuing Job Cards to 
beneficiaries, allocating employment and monitoring of works. Detailed 
provisions for planning, monitoring and evaluation, transparency, public 
accountability, social audit and conve rgence with other social sector 
programmes have been incorporated in the operational guidelines for 
NREGA. 
(iii) SAMPOORNAGRAMEEN ROZGAR YOJANA (SGRY) 
The Sampoorna Grammen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) is a wage 
employment scheme launched in September, 2001, and the Jawahar Gram 
Samridhi Yojana (JGSY) and Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS) were 
merged under this programme from First April 2002. The primary objective 
of the scheme is to provide additional wage employment in all rural areas 
and thereby provide food security and improve nutritional levels. The 
secondary objective is the creation of durable community, social and 
economic assets and infrastructure de velopment in rural areas. A special 
component under SGRY provides foodgrains to calamity stricken states for 
undertaking relief activities. Thirty per cent of employment opportunities 
under the programme are reserved for women. The programme is 
implemented through the panchayat raj institutions (PRIs). 
Each zilla parishad/DRDA, intermediate level and village panchayat 
prepares an annual action plan to incl ude the works to be undertaken under 
the scheme. Completion of incomplete works is given priority and emphasis 
is laid on labour-intensive wo rks. Priority is to be given to soil and moisture 
conservation, minor irrigation, rejuvenation of drinking water sources, 
augmentation of ground water, traditional water harvesting structure, 
desiltation of village tanks/ponds, construction of rural link roads, drainage 
works, afforestation, school, kitc hen sheds for schools, dispensaries, 
community centres, panchayat ghars, development of haats (markets), etc. 
However, the nature of works should be such that they could be completed in 
one or two years. Up to a maximum of 15 per cent of the funds can be spent 
on maintenance of assets created under the programme by the zilla 
parishads/DRDAs/intermediate panchayats/village panchayats. 
(iv) NATIONAL FOOD FOR WORK PROGRAMME (NFFWP) 
The National Food for Work Programme was launched in 150 most 
backward districts of the country from November 2004. The objective of 
77 

RAJYA SABHA [2 March, 2006] 
the programme was to provide additional resources to 150 most backward districts 
of the country so that generation of supplementary wage employment and 
provision of food security through creation of need based economic, social and 
community assets in these districts is further intensified. With effect from 2nd 
February, 2006, the NREGAis operational in the 150 NFFWP districts. 
(v) INDIRA AWAAS YOJANA (IAY) 
The composite multi pronged strategy for housing has been 
operationalised w.e.f. 1999-2000. The Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) is the major 
scheme for construction of houses to be given to the poor, free of cost. It has an 
additional component, namely, conversion of unserviceable kutcha houses to 
semi pucca houses. Further, a Credit- cum-Subsidy Scheme for rural housing 
was launched from 1.4.1999 targetting rural families having annual income 
up to Rs. 32,000. 
The ceiling on construction assistance was revised on 1 April 2004 and 
currently is set at Rs. 25,000 per unit for the plain areas and Rs. 27,500 for 
the hilly/difficult areas. 
Statement-Ill 
Note on Urban Poverty Alleviation Programmes/Schemes 
In this regard, it is informed that a monitorable target of reduction of 
poverty ratio by 5 percentage point by 2007 has been fixed in the Tenth Five 
Year Plan. However, there is no specific mention about Urban poverty. Further, it is 
informed that the progress of Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) 
which is the only poverty alleviation scheme, rests with the Ministry itself. In 
addition to this, VAMBAY and NSDP programmes which are meant for 
providing shelter/upgradation of shelter and environmental upgradation for 
the urban slum dwellers, also contribute indirectly towards poverty 
alleviation. The scheme/programme-wise details are given below:— 
SJSRY— Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rojgar Yojana (SJSRY) is a 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) which is funded on 75:25 basis between 
Centre and States. This scheme is continuing since 1997-98 & is the only 
scheme for urban employment aims to provide gainful employment through 
setting up of self-employment ventures or provisions of wage employment. 
78 

[2 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
During the first four years of the tenth plan, Rs. 493 crore is expected to be 
utilized as against the Tenth plan allocation of Rs. 541 crore. This is a demand-
driven scheme, however, an annual target of 80,000 under self 
employment/Development of Women and Child in Urban Areas (subsidy 
component) and 1 lakh persons under the training component have been fixed 
by the Ministry of Urban Employment and Poverty Alleviation. During the 
first three years of the Tenth Plan, 297419 persons have been provided self-
employment while 327399 persons have been trained during the same period as 
reported by the Ministry. 
VAMBAY— The Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY) was 
introduced in 2001-02 to meet the long-standing gap in programmes for slum-
dwellers, viz provision of a shelter or upgrading the existing shelter of people 
living below the poverty line in urban slums. Under VAMBAY, Govt, of India 
provides 50% central subsidy while the states have the option to obilize its 
matching portion of 50% from other sources, such as their own budget 
provision, resources of local bodies, loans from other agencies, contributions 
from beneficiaries or NGOs etc. Under this scheme, 20% of the total 
allocation is provided for sanitation and community toilets to be built for the 
urban poor and slum dwellers. 
During the first four years of the Tenth Plan, Rs. 975.31 crore 
expected to be utilized under the scheme as against the Tenth Plan allocation 
of Rs. 2043 crore. Against the target of 1 lakh, 1.06 lakh and 1.12 lakh 
dwelling units under VAMBAY for the first three years of the Tenth Plan, 
construction of 1,10,388, 1,08,376 and 1,13,004 dwelling units respectively 
were covered. 
NSDP— National Slum Developmen t Programme which is an ACA 
scheme under the State Sector meant for providing shelter and 
environmental upgradation for the urban slum dwellers. Out of the allocation 
of Rs. 1429 crore, an amount of Rs. 1282.30 was released and an expenditure 
of Rs. 866.99 crore has been reported during the first three years of the Tenth 
Plan under NSDP. Since the inception of the scheme from 1996-97 and up to 
2004-05 (as on 30.6.2005), 413.06 lakh persons covering 68129 slum pockets in 
2573 towns were benefited under the scheme.

proofing, livelihood support, connectivity, health, education, etc. as per local 
priorities. This component covers eight districts of the KBK region, namely, 
Koraput, Malkangiri, Nawrangpur, Rayagada, Bolangir, Sonepur, Kalahandi 
and Nuapada.An allocation of Rs. 250 crore per annum is being made for this 
component, (iii) Backward Districts Initiative covering 147 districts including 32 
districts affected by left wing extr emism. The main objectives of this 
component are to address the problems of low agricultural productivity, 
unemployment and to fill critical gaps in physical and social infrastructure. The

a District Plan consisting of schemes to achieve these objectives. A sum of Rs. 15 
crore is to be provided to each district annually over a period of three years i.e. a

satisfactory progress of the District Plan. The list of 147 districts covered under 
this component is enclosed as Statement. (See below)

Definition of Village Electrification 
A new definition of village electrification has been notified and has 
become effective from year 2004-05.

lines are provided in the habited locality as well as the Dalit Basti/hamlet 
where it exists. (For electrification through Non-Conventional Energy 
Sources a Distribution Transformer may not be necessary).

Health Centres, Dispensaries, Community Centers etc. and 
(iii) The number of households electrified should be at least 10% of the 
total number of households in the village.

Power consumers in Delhi 
1092. SHRI R.K. ANAND: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that on an average, 30 lakh billed power 
consumers in Delhi had paid about Rs. 5000/- this year for power that others 
have stolen; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the billed consumers had to pay for 
guaranteeing a 16 percent return on any investments private distributors make; 
and 
(c) if so, who is responsible for putting the interests of innocent 
consumer at the whims and wishes of private power distribution companies 
and what safeguards would be initiated to check it? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) 
The electricity sector in Delhi is a regulated business and it is governed by an 
independent regulator, Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission (DERC). The 
consumer is required to pay the chargesfof the consumption of electricity based 
upon the tariff approved by the DERC from time to time. While fixing tariff 
the level of Aggregate Technical & Commercial losses is also taken into 
consideration. In some of the pockets AT&C loss level is still more than 
50%. 
(b) As per the policy directions of Government of NCT of Delhi, 16% 
return on the issued and paid up capital and free reserves (excluding consumer 
contribution and revaluation reserves but including share premium and 
retained profits outstanding at the end of any particular 
107

year) is admissible to the licensee prov ided that such share capital and free 
reserves have been invested into fixed or any other assets, which have been put 
into beneficial use for the purpose of electricity distribution and retail supply and 
provided further that such investment of such share capital and free reserves has 
the approval of the Commi ssion. These policy directions are applicable only 
for first five years of privatization beginning 1st July, 2002. 16% return is 
available only when the licensee has achieved the committed levels of AT&C 
loss reduction. Further the distribution licensee's returns are adversely affected 
if it fails to achieve the set targets. 
(c) For safeguarding the interests of consumers, the DERC, inter alia, 
monitors the following:— 
• Loss reduction. 
• Properly incurred expenses in approving tariff 
• Performance standards. 
• Consumer grievance redressal.

Open access in power sector 
1095. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the steps taken so far by the Central and State Governments, including the 
State Electricity Boards to introduce open access in the power generation, transmission 
and dustribution sector; 
(b) the private sectors response, so far, in the transmission sector, >n ins power 
generation sector, especially the hydro-power generation; 
(c) whether it is a fact that private sector is interested particularly in the distribution 
sector, where they have direct inter-face with the poor consumer and collect easy 
money? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) The 
Electricity Act, 2003 has delicensed generation. It provides for open access in 
transmission from the very beginning. The Act provides for phased introduction of 
open access in distribution by the State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs). 
The Act provides that the State Commission shall, not later than 27th January, 2009, by 
regulations, provide such open access to all consumers who require a supply of 
electricity where the maximum power to be made available at any time exceeds one 
megawatt. 
The Tariff Policy suggests that in whichever states the situation so permits, the 
Regulatory Commissions should introduce open access even prior to this deadline. The 
policy lays down the methodology for computation of cross subsidy surcharge. 
The National Electricity Policy stresses on the need to provide facilitative 
frame-work by the Regulatory Commissions for non-discriminative open 
access. 
The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) had already issued 
regulations on grant of open access in inter-state transmission. At the State level, 19 
SERCs have issued final regulations and 2 SERCs have issued draft regulations on open 
access in distribution. 
As per information available, applications for grant of open access in distribution 
have been received in various States and seven cases of

Himachal Pradesh.

(b) and (c) Keeping in view the sensitivity of the need to reform and 
revitalizing of the power sector, changes have been incorporated in the 
implementation of Accelerated Power Development and Reforms 
Programme (APDRP) from time to time. The changes have been based not only 
on the requirement but also on the basis of feedback received from various 
stakeholders in the power sector. They are: 
(i) APDRP was originally started as Accelerated Power Development 
Programme (APDP) in 2000-01, with emphasis on upgradation of 
sub-transmission and distribution network and also on renovation 
and modernization/life extension/uprating of old power plants (thermal 
and hydel). 
(ii) Based on the resolutions passed in the Chief Ministers' conference 
held on March 3, 2001 and recommendations of Deepak Parekh 
Committee on Staie specific reforms APDP was rechristened as 
APDRP during 2002-03 with focus on concentrated zones i.e. 
industrial and urban areas. Incentive component was introduced in 
2002-03 to encourage the utilities to reduce their cash losses. 
(iii) To make the programme more effective, the following measures were 
initiated: 
♦ the utilities were asked to sign Memorandum of Agreement 
(MOA), to commit improvements in set of benchmark 
parameters. 
♦ Linking of securitisation under Tripartite Agreement to secure 
CPSUs dues for assistance under APDRP. 
♦ A massive programme for training of utility personnel. 
♦ Ranking of SEBs/utilities by independent agencies viz CRISIL 
&ICRA. 
♦ Dissemination of best practices amongst the utilities through 
national level workshops. 
♦ Appointing agencies like TERI (The Energy & Resources 
Institute), SBI Capital, Tata Consultancy Services, Indian 
Institute of Management, Ahmedabad (IIMA) and ASCI 
(Administrative Staff College of India), Hyderabad to evaluate 
APDRP projects. 
123

The main features of programme are to reduce Aggregate Technical and Commercial 
(AT & C) losses; to bring about commercial viability; to reduce outages and interruptions;

component that covers strengthening and upgradation of sub-transmission and 
distribution system with twenty five percent grant and an incentive component as grant 
to states/utilities that reduce cash losses with 2000-01 as the base year. 
Thus, restructuring the Accelerated Power Development and Reforms 
Programme (APDRP) is a continuous process not only to fine-tune the parameters of 
performance of the power utilities but also to motivate the power utilities to become

Monsoon forecasting agencies 
1107. SHRI R.K. ANAND: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Indian Meterological Department and the CSIR 
for Mathematical modelling and computer simulation have given two different 
monsoon forecasts; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) whether the gadgets used for predicting monsoon in India are primitive and 
require change and the reasons forwhich these two agencies don't share their expertise? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) 
Yes, Sir. The mandate for issuing long range monsoon forecast for the country rests with 
India Meteorological Department (IMD). IMD uses a statistical model for monsoon 
forecast. Centre for Mathematical Modelling and Computer Simulation (C-MMACS) is 
conducting studies on monsoon forecast and uses a dynamical model on experimental basis. 
Studies have shown that dynamical models have not evolved to a stage where they can 
simulate the year to year monsoon rainfall realistically. 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [2 March, 2006] 
Therefore, IMD which has been historically depending on the statistical model 
have not yet adopted dynamical model for making forecast. More test and 
research work is required to switchover to dynamical model for making 
monsoon forecast by IMD. 
(b) C-MMACS issued fo recasts for June, July and August months 
separately. Prediction made by C-MMA CS for June rainfall was below 
normal by 34%, prediction for July 2005 was12% below normal and for 
AugusJ, 13% above normal. Actual ra infall in June 2005 was 12% below 
normal, in July 14% above normal and in August 27% below normal. 
IMD's forecast for the seasonal rainfall over the country as a whole was 
2% below normal which was very close to actual seasonal rainfall (1% below 
normal).

Monsoon prediction 
1114. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact there is no improvement in the predictions of monsoon in 
India since early 1930s; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have studied the recurring failures in predicting 
droughts and floods; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) 
and (b) No, Sir. India Meteorological Department (IMD) has been issuing operational 
long range forecasts based on objective statistical models since late 1920s. 
From 1924 to 1987, India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued forecasts 
for two broad homogeneous region (NW India and Peninsula). During this period, on 
an average, the percentage of correct forecasts ranged between 58% to 63%. Since 1988, 
IMD has prepared forecasts for southwest monsoon rainfall over the country as a whole. 
During the period 1988—2005, all the forecasts (for the country as a whole) were 
generally correct except in drought year of 2002 and 2004, when rainfall received 
were in the deficient category against forecast of normal rainfall. It may be mentioned, that 
no operational forecasting group (either in India or abroad) could predict the droughts of 
2002 and 2004. IMD's forecasts for 2005 southwest monsoon rainfall was proved 
correct. 
(c) and (d) There are no techniques available at present to predict droughts in 
advance. They are being dynamically monitored. IMD provides necessary inputs on rainfall 
distribution of all meteorological subdivisions to the concerned agencies during the 
monsoon season. This helps in mobilizing resources to combat the evolving drought 
scenarios. 
IMD also provides necessary meteorological inputs to Central Water Commission, 
which is the nodal agency for flood forecasting. However, forecast of heavy rainfall which 
may lead to flood situations is done only in short range time scale. 
140 

[2 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
For improving Long rage forecasting of monsoon rainfall, India 
Meteorological Department has been making critical review of its predictions 
regularly, especially after the failure in 2002 and 2004. IMD has taken the following 
major steps to improve its monsoon prediction capability. 
• Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore is collaborating with IMD and helping 
to implement a dynamical prediction system using the mathematical model 
developed at the Experimental Climate Prediction Centre, scripps Institute of 
Oceanography, USA. This model has shown reasonable skill in predicting 
monsoon rainfall over India. Using this model, experimental forecasts 
were prepared for the 2005 southwest monsoon rainfall. However, 
more.quality tests and research work are required before the model can be put 
to use for operation of work. 
• As statistical models outperform dynamical models at present, IMD has 
developed many new statistical models with the aim to replace existing 
operational statistical models. These new statistical models have shown 
improved skill but have to be tested for a couple of years more before their use in 
operational mode. 
(e) Doesn't arise.

1133. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of STATISTICS AND

calculating the GDP after a gap of ten y ears to a gap of six years to proejct

AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI G.K. VASAN): (a) and 
(b) In the past, National Accounts Statistics were revised decennially using 
the information on working force from the Population Census. However, in the 
previous series of national accounts with the base year 1993-94 (introduced in 
February, 1999), the workforce data from the Quinquennial Employment and 
Unemployment Survey, 1993-94 conducted by the National sample survey 
Organisation (NSSO) in its 50th round was used, as it was observed that data on

round Quinquennial Employment and Unemployment Servey in 1999-2000.

1137. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of URBAN

161

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIAJAY MAKEN): (a) to  (c) Yes, Sir. This Ministry 
gives top priority for improvement of water management system in urban areas 
to ensure an efficient and sustained water supply system and services. Top 
priority is also attached to sector reforms, namely, institutional and financial 
reforms including capacity building to ensure efficient management of water 
supply system in urban areas. Model building bye-laws have been prepared 
and circulated to State Governments by the Town & Country Planning 
Organization to include water conserva tion measures such as rain water 
harvesting, reuse and recycle of waste water in urban areas. A Manual on 
operation & Maintenance of Water Supply Systems has been published by 
Ministry of Urban Development for planning and designing various 
components of water supply systems to help personnel involved in execution 
and maintenance of water supply proj ects. The Manual also deals with 
qualitative aspects of treated water for drinking purpose. 
Ministry of Urban Development has already launched Jawaharlal Nehru 
National Urban Renewal Mission and Urban Infrastructure Development 
Scheme for Small and Medium Towns for providing reform-linked central 
assistance to cities & towns. The main objective is to secure effective linkages 
between asset creation and asset management so that the water supply services 
created in the cities are not only maintained efficiently but also become self-
sustaining over a period of time. Some of the mandatory reforms to be 
undertaken at ULB and/or state leve l are adoption of modern, accrual-based 
double entry system of accounting, introduction of system of e-governance 
using IT applications, levy of reasonable user charges with the objective that 
full cost of operation and maintenance of recurring cost is collected, etc. Some 
of the optional reforms to be implemented at the state and/or ULB level are 
revision of bye-laws to make rain water harvesting mandatory in all 
buildings, adoption of water conservation measures, structural reforms, 
public private partnership etc. These reforms are expected to improve water 
management system in urban areas.

(b) The Mission objectives of JNNURM are: 
i) Focussed attention to integrated development of infrastructure services in the 
cities covered under the Mission. 
ti) Secure effective linkages between asset creation and asset management so 
that the infrastructural services created in the cities are not only maintained 
efficiently but also become self-sustaining over time.

v) Scale up delivery of civic amenities and provision of utilities with emphasis 
on universal access to urban poor. 
vi) To take up urban renewal programme, i.e. re-development of inner (old) 
cities area to reduce congestion. 
Objectives of UIDSSMT are: 
i) Improve infrastructural facilities and help create durable public assets and 
quality oriented services in cities & towns 
ii) Enhance public-private partnership in infrastructural development and 
iii) Promote planned integrated development of towns and cities.

these reforms are to be carried out within mission period of 7 years. 
Statement-I 
List of Mandatory reforms 
There will be two sets of mandatory reforms. Core reforms at ULB/ Parastatal 
level aims at process re-engineering through deployment of technology to enable 
more efficient, reliable, timely services in a transparent manner. The other set of 
reforms are framework related at State level. 
1.1 Urban Local Body/Parastatai level Reforms: 
i. Adoption of modern, accrual-based double entry system of accounting 
in Urban Local Bodies/Parastatals. 
ii. Introduction of system of e-governance using IT appflcations like, GIS and MIS 
for various services provided by ULBs/Parastatals. 
iii. Reform of property tax with GIS, so that it becomes major source of revenue 
for Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and arrangements for its effective 
implementation so that collection efficiency reaches at least 85% within 
next seven years. 
iv Levy of reasonable user charges by ULBs/Parastatals with the objective that 
full cost of operation and maintenance or recurring cost is collected within next 
seven years. However, cities/towns in North East and other special category 
States may recover at least 50% of operation & maintenance charges 
initially. These cities/towns should graduate to full O&M cost recovery in 
a phased manner. 
v. Internal earmarking within local body, budgets for basic services to the urban 
poor. 
vi. Provision of basic services to urban poor including security of tenure at 
affordable prices, improved housing, water supply, sanitation and ensuing 
delivery of other already existing universal services of the Government for 
education, health and social security. 
181

ii. "Repeal of Urban Land Ceiling and Regulation Act.

1160. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that a large proportion (26 per cent or 
260 million) of Indians are still Below the Poverty Line as per India's first Social 
Development Report released, recently; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the poverty levels have shown a decline and there is 
huge disparity among the social classes with the percentage of the poor among the 
Scheduled Tribes being 43.8 per cent, Scheduled Castes 36.2 per cent and Other 
backward Classes 21 per cent; and 
(c) if so, the efforts Government propose to make to harness the nation's social 
energy to ensure a fair and equitable process of development? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA):'(a) Yes, Sir. 
As per the recently released India's first Social Development Report, 260 million 
Indians are still below the poverty line, according to 1999-2000 data (page no. 2, Table 
No. 1.1 of the Report). It may be mentioned that this figure is taken from the official 
poverty estimates 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [2 March, 2006] 
brought out by the Planning Commission on the basis of NSS 55th round of large scale 
sample survey on household consumer expenditure, which was conducted during the 
year 1999-2000. 
(b) The incidence of poverty has declined from 36.0% to 26.1% from 1993-94 
to 1999-2000 and the decline in number of persons below poverty line in absolute term 
has come down from 320.3 million to 260.2 million. From the latest available data of 
large scale sample survey on household consumer expenditure conducted by the 
NSSO (National Sample Survey Organization) during the year 1999-2000, the percentage 
of Scheduled Tribes living below poverty line is 45.86% and 34.75% in rural and urban 
areas respectively, and the percentage of Scheduled Castes living below poverty line is 
36.25% and 38.47% in rural and urban areas respectively. 
(c) Government of India have launched several development oriented 
poverty alleviation schemes/programmes like Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana 
(SJSRY), Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY), National Slum 
Development Programme (NSDP) etc. The recently launched Jawaharlal Nehru 
National Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM) strives for a Mission approach in tackling 
the issue of overall infrastructure development and basic amenities to the poor living in urban 
areas in the country.

1173.    SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: 
SHRI BALAVANT alias BALAPTE: 
Will the Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Sports Federations have been allotted funds for improving the 
performance and practices of sports persons; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether many Sports Federations have misused the funds allocated to 
them during the last two years; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; 
(e) whether Government have taken any action against such federations for 
misutilisation of funds during the last three years; 
(f) if so, the details thereof; and 
(g) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) The funds allotted to the recognised National Sports 
Federations for improving the performance of sports persons/teams during the last three 
years are detailed in the Statement. (See below) 
(c) to (g) National Sports Federations (NSFs) are autonomous societies 
registered under the Societies Registration Act 1860. The Government of India 
provides assistance to recognized NSFs for organizing national and international 
events in India, participation in international tournaments abroad, procurement of 
equipment, training of national teams/sports-persons under Indian/foreign coaches, etc. 
There have been some complaints against NSFs about misuse of funds received from the 
Government. Any complaint against any NSF about misuse of funds etc. is processed 
promptly after ascertaining the comments of the NSF concerned. To ensure proper 
utilization of Government assistance, utilization certificates and statements of 
accounts duly audited by chartered accountants are required to be submitted and further 
assistance is released only on receipt of these documents. Further, this Ministry has issued 
sanction for audit through the Comptroller & Auditor General of India of NSFs getting 
assistance exceeding Rs. one crore in a year.

Bhandara, had taken loan for purchasing a tractor. The debt had

[2 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHR! 
MURLI DEORA):   Sir, I move: 
"That the Bill to provide for the establishment of Petroleum 
and Natural Gas Regulatory Board to regulate the 
refining, processing, storage, transportation, distribution, 
marketing and sale of petroleum, petroleum products and 
natural gas excluding production of crude oil and natural 
gas so as to protect the interests of consumers and 
entities engaged in specified activities relating to 
petroleum, petroleum products and natural gas and to 
ensure uninterrupted and adequate supply of petroleum, 
petroleum products and natural gas in all parts of the 
country and to promote competitive markets and for 
matters connected therewith or  incidental thereto, be 
taken into consideration.'' 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, my predecessor had Introduced a Bill 
entitled The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board 6tt, 2005' in 
this august House on 21" December , 2005. I seek the leave of the 
House for taking up this Bill for consideration. 
Before I come to the specifics of this Bill, I would like to state 
briefly the importance of the oil and gas sector in our growing economy. 
Energy is an essential requirement for economic development and it is 
an important pre-requistte for improving the quality of life of the people.   
At present, in the primary commercial energy mix of our country, coal, oil 
and gas constitute about 51 per cent, 36 per cent and 9 per cent 
respectively, with the balance four  per cent being met by the other 
sources.  As per the Hydrocarbon Vaion-2025, the combined share of 
oil and gas in the total energy mix in 2025 is likely to remain at the 
current level of 45 per cent. Our economy is poised to grow by over 8 
per cent during 2005-06 and this trend of robust growth is projected to 
continue in the foreseeable future. We import more than 70 per cent of 
our crude oil requirements to meet the dom estic demand of petroleum 
products. Further, at present, about only 50 per cent of the estimated 
gas demand is met by indigenous production. Thus, meeting the oil 
and gas requirements of our growing economy is a d aunting task. The 
National Common Minimum Programme emphasizes the need to put in 
place policies to enhance the country's energy security. The efforts 
made by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas in enhancing the oil 
and gas security of the country include - facilitating increase in domestic 
oil and gas production under the New Exploration and Licensing 
Policy, 
225 

RAJYA SABHA [2 March, 2006] 
acquiring oil and gas acreages abroad, facilitating LNG imports, taking 
initiative to import gas through transnational pipelines, diversifying 
crude oil supply sources, and taking steps to build strategic crude oil 
storage. 
The different sectors of the Indian economy have 
progressively moved towards the market-driven regimes in the past 
few years. In the sectors requir ing regulatory intervention, viz., 
electricity, telecom, etc., statutor y regulators have been established. 
Not only has this facilitated the much-needed investments in these 
sectors and their orderly growth , the consumers have benefited on 
account of availability of better serv ices and products at competitive 
prices. 
Through this Bill, the Government is envisaging to set up a 
statutory downstream petroleum a nd natural gas regulator with the 
following main objectives: 
to regulate the refining, processing, storage, 
transportation, distribution, marketing and sale of 
petroleum, petroleum products and natural gas so as to 
protect the interests of consumers and entities engaged in 
specified activities relating to petroleum, petroleum 
products and natural gas; 
to ensure uninterrupted  and adequate supply of 
petroleum, petroleum products and natural gas in all parts 
of the country; 
to promote competitive markets. 
Sir, earlier, in the 13 th Lok Sabha, the then Minister for 
Petroleum and Natural Gas had introduced "The Petroleum 
Regulatory Board Bill, 2002" in the Lok Sabha on the 6 th May, 2002. 
On the 17 th May, 2002, the Bill was referred to the Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Petroleum and Chemicals for examination 
and report. The Committee presented its report to the Lok Sabha 
about a year later, on the 8lh May, 2003, recommending that the Bill be 
passed, subject to their recommendations and observations. The 
official amendments, as proposed by the Committee, were introduced 
by the earlier. Government in the 14th session of the 13th Lok Sabha in 
December, 2003. However, the Bill could not be taken up for 
consideration by the 13th Lok Sabha, and it lapsed. 
The Parliamentary Standing Committee had made 49 
recommendations. The Government have accepted 47 of the 49 
recommendations by making appropriate modifications in the Bill in 
respect of 26 recommendations and incorporating 21   
recommendations in the 
226 

[2 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
rules/regulations which would be framed by the Government and Regulatory 
Board. With respect to the remaining two recommendations relating to 
declaring storage facilities, hydrant systems at airports, etc., as common 
carriers, the Bill introduced in this House on 21" December, 2005 seeks to 
empower the Board to register entities which propose to establish storage 
facilities for petroleum, petroleum products and natural gas beyond a 
certain capacity. The Ministry has generally agreed with the 
recommendations of the entire Committee. 
The Standing Committee had strongly recommended that the 
Government should lay down sepa rate regulations incorporating 
provisions essential to handling the specific problems of the gas 
sector. Our Government fully agrees with this recommendation. The 
petroleum and gas sectors are at different stages of development in the 
country, with the gas sector being at a nascent stage of growth. 
Globally, the share of natural gas in world's primary energy consumption 
is growing faster than the other commercial energy forms. It is often said 
that if oil was the fuel for the 20th century, the 21* century will be the era of 
gas. The Hydrocarbon Vision -2025 projects that the share of natural 
gas in the total energy mix in the country will increase to 20 per cent by 
the year 2025. With a view to incorporating the recommendations of 
the Standing Committee relating to the gas sector in the Bill, the 
Government had extensive consultations with the gas industry and we 
have incorporated appropriate provisions in the Bill, which specifically 
pertain to the gas sector. These relate, inter alia, to: (i) affiliate code of 
conduct; (ii) pipeline access code; ( iii) introduction of the concept of 
contract carrier; (iv) marketing servic e obligations of city or local gas 
distribution entities; (v) exclusivity for ascertain period for building or 
operating city or local gas distribution network; and (vi) methodology for 
fixation of transportation tariffs. 
It may be noted that while the Bill introduced in the Parliament 
in May, 2002 was titled "The Petroleum Regulatory Board pill, 2002", 
the present Bill is "The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Bill, 
2005". 
In addition to the changes related to the gas sector, a few 
refinements brought about in the present Bill relate to: (i) having a Member 
(Legal or Judicial) on the Board; (if) introduction of the concept of 'restrictive 
trade practices' instead of 'profiteering'; (iii) a common Appellate Tribunal 
for the electricity and petroleum sectors; (iv) deleting the exclusion of the 
jurisdiction of the MRTP Commiss ion/Competition Commission; etc.; 
(v) empowering the Board to register, instead of authorize, the entities 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [2 March, 2006] 
seeking to market petroleum products and setting up Liquefied Natural 
Gas Terminals; and (vi) registration of entities seeking to establish 
storage facilities beyond a certain capacity. 
In respect of laying common or contract carrier pipelines and for 
laying city or local gas distribution networks, the provision of authorization 
by Board has been retained. 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I would Ike to convey our thanks to the 
Chairman and Members of the Standing Committee for their 
contribution and valuable suggestions which helped in framing of the Bid, 
and also to the other stakeholders. 
Sir, I now commend the BM to this august House for consideration 
and passing. Thank you.
